title: I had dinner at one of Scotland's most haunted hotels - here's how it went
excerpt: Ahead of Halloween, food and drink writer Sarah Campbell dines at one of Scotland's most haunted hotels.
content:
The glow of a full moon is spilling through the clouds on a fierce, blustery night as we make our way along the winding roads around Loch Lomond.

There are just days to go until Halloween, and despite Storm Boelo's best efforts to scupper our spooky plans with power cuts and downed trees, we’re finally on track for dinner at one of not just Scotland’s but the UK's most haunted hotels.

For anyone with an interest in supernatural goings-on, The Drovers Inn, first established in 1705, will need little introduction, while those less clued up on its chilling lore need only take a look at this roadside stop's website to find all manner of testimony from former guests claiming to have encountered ghostly apparitions during their stays.

Our headlights sweep across the empty rooms on the hotel's upper floors as we pull into the car park, prompting a shiver down my scaredy-cat spine that has nothing to do with the weather. It's all a wee bit eerie, and I steal only a fleeting glance at the windows, half afraid a shadowy figure might be watching us right back.

After bundling into the main reception room, bar and restaurant, however, any sense of tension is instantly dispelled by the sheer exuberance of the team’s decorating efforts.

'Our bar area, although dark and small, is full of character and Scottish charm', the Drovers Inn team says (Image: Newsquest)

No surface has been left un-spiderwebbed, plastic severed limbs litter the landing and even the hotel’s famous collection of taxidermy animals has been given a ghoulish makeover befitting the occasion.

"Have you seen our two-headed lamb?" the bartender asks gleefully later as a tourist enquires as to whether any of the other beasts frozen into threatening poses for all eternity are real.

A sentence I can hand on heart say I've never heard before while on the job, but one that barely raises an eyebrow here.

Sharing the bar with a few solo travellers and families in waterproofs who seem thankful for the warmth of the open fire crackling in the corner, we take a moment to debate which pub grub picks will make for the most fruitful review fodder.

"I don't think this is the sort of place that people come to have a cauliflower steak," Gaz counters when I suggest that might be the most adventurous of choices.

With apologies to any veggie readers, he has a point. There's an old-school vibe at The Drovers, reinforced by pots of individual sauce sachets and plastic-capped salt and pepper shakers on each of the tables. It doesn’t take a psychic to suggest that the likes of steak and Guinness pie or homemade mince and tatties will be among the best-sellers here. Although, incidentally, the team does have one booked for readings as part of this weekend’s celebrations.

"Fine," I concede, "but let's definitely get the gravlax then."

Roast supreme of chicken with chips and a whisky cream jus (Image: Newsquest)

In a violent fuchsia hue that’s closer to pickled beetroot than smoked salmon, these gummy slices of fish (£8.50) are hit and miss. Some are just right, soft and supple in the centre but gently chewy towards their candied edges, while others are stringy and fibrous, a texture not helped by rounds of crostini stiff enough to crack rather than crunch.

A haggis, neeps and tatties starter (Image: Newsquest)

A lesson in the perils of straying too far from the failsafe, further driven home by the starter-sized serving of haggis, neeps and tatties (£7.95) on the other side of the table.

Here, everything works in seamless, satisfying harmony, from the punchy whisky and peppercorn sauce to cubes of sweet root veg scattered over crumbly meat pudding and lush mashed potato. Exactly the sort of food you want to be eating while the wind howls on the other side of thick stone walls.

Mac and cheese with garlic bread and side salad (Image: Newsquest)

On that same par is the mac and cheese (£13.95), piled into a deep oval dish generously enough to induce a carb coma so profound that not even the paranormal activity upstairs could disturb your slumber. Beneath a blanket of cheddar grilled into an even crust lies a mild, sturdy cheese sauce clinging to tubes of pasta that have bubbled until soft and bloated, while a small, dressed side salad cancels out any guilt over a piece of garlic-butter-drenched bread.

Just when I'm starting to think I've got a handle on the Drovers Inn kitchen's no-frills, no-frights style, the supreme of chicken (£16.50) arrives looking closer to gastropub territory than we've dared to venture so far. Stacked high on the plate is a medley of roast carrots, broccoli, asparagus and somewhat less nutritious chunky chips, all drowned in a glug of whisky cream jus. Meat served on the bone is surprisingly juicy under its crisped outer skin, and overall this main course strikes a happy middle ground between the overreaching gravlax and comfort food classics elsewhere.

Sticky toffee pudding with vanilla ice cream (Image: Newsquest)

The meal cruises to its close with a sticky toffee pudding (£7.65) that's all but obligatory in a rural pub setting like this. It’s not quite as decadent as the spiced, squidgy, date-filled sponge you might hope for, but still ticks most of the right boxes, slicked with glossy toffee sauce and finished with a scoop of sweet vanilla ice cream.

We're keen to go in search of that aforementioned two-headed lamb before heading back out into the tail end of the storm, so tear ourselves away from the snug comfort of the bar just as staff are discussing the cocktail specials they're planning to serve on Halloween weekend.

Spaces for these special events are already fully booked, social media later reveals, and that’s no surprise. It's difficult to imagine many other places in the country that are quite so atmospheric at this time of year.

And, for all its hair-raising first impressions on arrival, there's really nothing to fear at the Drovers Inn's bar and restaurant beyond perhaps a run-in with its stuffed grizzly bear after one too many whiskies.

With such a fine, characterful haunt to call home, it's little wonder all of its ghosts have stuck around for centuries.

Menu: It's pub grub classics with a couple of more adventurous options like salmon gravlax or cauliflower steak. 3/5

Service: Orders are placed at the bar, but the team is friendly and proud to show off the inn's quirky character. 4/5

Atmosphere: There's surely no better place to celebrate Halloween than at one of Scotland's most haunted pubs, where the team has gone all out with decorations. 5/5

Price: Generous portions throughout mean you certainly won't leave feeling short-changed, even if quality occasionally dips. 4/5

Food: Having just reopened hours earlier following a temporary closure during Storm Boelo power cuts, the kitchen is back on form and at its best when leaning into comfort food. 7/10

Total: 23/30

The Drovers Inn is located in Inverarnan, North Loch Lomond.

Sarah Campbell is The Herald’s Food and Drink writer and restaurant critic. You can find her on X or Instagram @sz_campbell.
